sources.news_title: Trump says Ireland unification is ‘going to happen eventually’
sources.text:
Trump says he would ‘love’ to see a united Ireland — just days after new UK PM said it was off the table
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
President Trump said he would “love” to see a unified Ireland – and predicted during his trip to the Emerald Isle Saturday that a merger between Republican of Ireland and Northern Ireland is “going to happen eventually.”
The president’s comments come days after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the UK was “off the table.”
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified. I have friends on both sides, great people,” Trump said when asked about the controversial topic on his two-day trip.
“They’re Irish people. How can they be bad, right? I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously, but I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
The 1998 Good Friday Agreement empowers the British government to call such a referendum, and requires a majority vote in both Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland before unification can happen.
Northern Ireland has been under British rule since 1921.
Unification wasn’t the only UK issue Trump waded into on his trip.
He also spoke about the Falkland Islands, days after telling GB News he might not help if Argentina sought to seize the territory. Trump has been seething at the UK and other NATO allies for failing to provide sufficient assistance to the war in Iran.
Tensions are on an upswing between the two nations over the British territory, and Trump ally Argentinian President Javier Millei said in a speech last week that the islands “are our future.”
While appearing with Irish Toiseach Micheal Martin, Trump was asked about a recent conversation with Burnham and whether the Falklands – long claimed by Argentina – came up.
“I remember as a young boy, pretty young boy anyway, the Falkland Islands,” Trump said, referencing the 1982 conflict. Then he appeared to say the UK would have difficulty repelling a Falklands invasion by Argentina.
“I don’t know if they’re going to be willing to travel that far. That is very far away. You’re talking about weeks by boat,” Trump said, adding that he might consider playing a mediating role.
“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster.”
The president is set to travel later Saturday to his Doonbeg golf course in County Clare, where he is attending the Irish Open.

sources.news_title: Trump Says Irish Unification Would Be ‘Fantastic,’ Says It ‘May as Well Happen Now’
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said during a visit to Dublin that he would “love to see” Northern Ireland reunified with the Republic of Ireland, calling the prospect “fantastic” while acknowledging that the United Kingdom would have a decisive role in any change.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
President Donald Trump publicly embraced the prospect of a united Ireland on Saturday, breaking with the traditionally neutral posture of U.S. presidents on one of the most politically sensitive questions in British and Irish affairs.
Speaking alongside Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin following talks in Dublin, Trump said he believed reunification of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland would ultimately occur and questioned why it should be postponed.
“The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now,” Trump told reporters.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said, while adding that “the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.” Trump later acknowledged that there was “no good answer” to the question while again describing Irish unity as “a very cool thing.”
The comments represented a notable departure from the caution traditionally exercised by American presidents on Northern Ireland’s constitutional status. The United States played an important role in the peace process that produced the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, but previous administrations generally avoided taking a position on whether Northern Ireland should remain in the United Kingdom or join the Republic of Ireland.
Ireland has been politically divided for more than a century, with Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom while the remainder of the island became what is now the Republic of Ireland.
The Good Friday Agreement, reached after three decades of violence known as the Troubles, established the principle that Northern Ireland’s constitutional future must be determined through democratic consent. A border poll must be called if the U.K. secretary of state for Northern Ireland concludes that a majority appears likely to favor joining a united Ireland. Reunification would ultimately require majority support in both Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month that a unity referendum was “off the table.” Downing Street reiterated Saturday that the government’s position had not changed following Trump’s remarks.
Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, whose party supports Northern Ireland remaining in the United Kingdom, rejected Trump’s prediction.
“As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic,” Robinson wrote on X.
Robinson separately emphasized that Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its own population rather than outside governments.
Trump’s comments came during a two-day visit combining official meetings in Dublin with an appearance at the Irish Open at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare.
The president arrived aboard the refurbished aircraft originally provided to the United States by Qatar, which had recently entered service as Air Force One. The trip prompted one of Ireland’s largest presidential security operations, involving nearly 4,000 police and other personnel and an estimated cost approaching 20 million euros.
Trump was received in Dublin by Irish President Catherine Connolly before meeting Martin. He inspected a military guard of honor during the official portion of the visit.
The discussions with Irish officials ranged beyond reunification, encompassing the war with Iran, U.S.-European trade, tariffs affecting pharmaceutical products and immigration. Ireland and the United States retain extensive economic and ancestral ties, with U.S.-owned companies representing a significant part of the Irish economy.
Their governments also differ sharply on several foreign-policy issues. Ireland has been among the European countries most critical of Israel’s conduct in Gaza and has supported restrictions targeting trade connected to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Connolly, who had participated in protests during Trump’s 2019 visit before becoming president, told Trump Saturday of what she described as “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted.”
Following his Dublin engagements, Trump traveled west to the Doonbeg property purchased by the Trump Organization in 2014, where some 40,000 spectators were expected over the weekend for the Irish Open. The tournament featured six-time major champion Rory McIlroy, currently ranked No. 2 in the world.
McIlroy, who has previously played golf with Trump, said ahead of the tournament that the president’s presence would inevitably make the event feel “different,” but said competitors intended to “keep our heads down and play.”
Trump’s attendance at a major international tournament hosted by a property bearing his name also renewed scrutiny of the overlap between presidential travel and his family’s business interests.
“He’s really just visiting the golf resort he owns and dropping into Dublin for a courtesy visit,” Daniel Geary, a U.S. history professor at Trinity College Dublin, said.
“He sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president.”
Trump has repeatedly incorporated his golf properties into high-profile activities since returning to office in January 2025. During a trip to Scotland last summer, he hosted then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at his Turnberry resort before inaugurating another Trump-branded course near Aberdeen.
He may also participate in Sunday’s Irish Open closing events, potentially including presentation of the tournament trophy.
But it was Trump’s statement on Irish unity that produced the most immediate political reaction Saturday.
Under the Good Friday Agreement, neither the U.S. president nor the Irish government can unilaterally change Northern Ireland’s constitutional status. That decision remains governed by the principle of consent and, ultimately, votes on both sides of the Irish border.
Trump nevertheless made his personal preference unusually explicit.
“I’d love to see it unified,” he said. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”

'How can it be bad?' US President Donald Trump would 'love' to see a united Ireland
US President Donald Trump has expressed that he would love to see Ireland reunited, adding ‘how can it be bad?’ as he spoke to media during his weekend visit.
The president was speaking publicly to the press as he met with Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House during his two-day visit to Ireland
When asked for his view, the President said: “Well I don’t want to cause any problems but I will tell you I would love to see it unified.
I have friends on both sides, great people. They're Irish people, ow can they be bad, right? I'd love to see it unified.

"You know what? The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”
Poitning to An Taoiseach, he added: “We were talking about it and you’ve got the right man here to get it moving. I think it would be a fantstic thing."
He added that he believed the UK would have something to say about it but added that he thought it would be “a great thing”.
"How can it be bad?” he added.
Derry’s SDLP MP and long-term critic of the Trump administration, Colum Eastwood shared a clip of the President’s comments on his social media afterwards on Saturday and quipped ‘Always liked him’.
Sinn Féin Leader Mary Lou McDonald meanwhile posted: “The US plays a critical role in supporting peace in Ireland. That same commitment to diplomacy & peace must be applied to Palestine. The US must stop arming Israel and stop facilitating the genocide.
“President Trump’s comments on Irish reunification are timely. The Taoiseach must now begin planning for a united Ireland.”
The development however led to criticism from Unionist leaders in the north.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson posted: “President Trump knows better than most that elections matter. Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.
“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident NI will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers
TUV leader Jim Allister said: “Donald Trump is not the first US President to meddle in the affairs which don’t concern him. At the 12th July demonstration in 1919 Edward Carson had occasion to observe in relation to the USA: ‘You attend to your own affairs and we will attend to ours. We will not brook interference in our affairs’.
"The message over 100 years later from Unionist leaders and indeed the people of Northern Ireland is the same. Northern Ireland not a pawn in Trump’s fall out with the UK. Our constitutional future does not depend on him or any other foreign dignitary.”
Meanwhile mass protests are taking place in the south during the President’s visit with a ‘Wanted’ billboard featuring his face also erected at Free Derry Corner.
Across the Atlantic, representatives from largest Irish American organisation in the United State, the Ancient Order of Hibernians, welcomed Trump’s remarks.
AOH National President Sean Pender and AOH Political Education Chair Neil F. Cosgrove also commented on recent utterances by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and unionists in the north in relation to the future border poll on Irish unity as enshrined in the Good Friday Agreement.
In a joint statement from the AOH headquarters in New York, they said: “For the Ancient Order of Hibernians, which has long supported Irish reunification through the democratic provisions of the Good Friday Agreement, the President’s remarks are welcome.
"The response from representatives of Unionist political parties has been sadly predictable: a selective reading of the Good Friday Agreement, an agreement their parties initially opposed, coupled with declarations that the future of Northern Ireland must be decided by the people of Northern Ireland. On that last point, we agree.
“If Unionist leaders truly believe that Northern Ireland’s future belongs in the hands of its people, they should have nothing to fear from clear criteria, transparent assessment, and an honest democratic process. One cannot champion the people’s right to decide while simultaneously opposing the democratic mechanism by which they are allowed to do so
“That is why recent comments from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham deserve closer scrutiny. He has said that he does not ‘see’ evidence that a border poll would pass. The obvious question is: is the British Government even looking? Not seeing evidence is not evidence of absence, particularly when the government has never established a transparent process for looking for it.
“The responsibility for determining whether the conditions for a border poll have been met rests with the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland. If the Secretary of State concludes that the statutory test has not been met, then the British Government should explain how that conclusion was reached. The right to self-determination and the constitutional future of an island of more than seven million people deserve more than a “gut feel.” They require credible and transparent criteria; criteria Whitehall has not revealed. London should not be able to postpone indefinitely the democratic mechanism through which the people of Ireland can determine their future.
“There is also the striking inconsistency of Prime Minister Burnham’s position. His government vigorously defends the right of the people of the Falkland Islands to determine their constitutional status, yet when the constitutional future of Northern Ireland is raised, a referendum is declared ‘off the table’. The principle of consent should not depend upon geography. A border poll should be called when the conditions established by the Good Friday Agreement and the Northern Ireland Act are met, not when doing so is politically convenient for Whitehall. Nor should the United States simply be dismissed as an outside voice with no legitimate interest in this discussion. American diplomacy was central to the peace process that produced the Good Friday Agreement, and successive administrations have remained engaged in defending that agreement and encouraging peace and prosperity in Northern Ireland.
“The Ancient Order of Hibernians therefore calls for President Trump’s welcome remarks to be followed by renewed American engagement, including the appointment of a U.S. Special Envoy for Northern Ireland. We further call upon the British Government to establish and publish a clear and transparent process for assessing when the statutory conditions for a border poll have been met.
"President Trump has expressed his view. British Prime Minister Burnham and the Northern Ireland Secretary have expressed theirs. The final decision does not belong to any of them. It belongs to the Irish people, it is time to give them the mechanism to express it.”
Earlier on Saturday, Uachtarán na hÉireann, Catherine Connolly, met with the President of the United States of America, Donald Trump, on a courtesy call at Áras an Uachtaráin.
In a statement following the meeting, President Connolly said: “As President of Ireland, I am very conscious that Ireland and the United States of America are bound by strong ties. This is a deep connection, built over centuries, which allows us to speak openly to one another.
“We are in a world facing the existential threat posed by war and climate change, both of which are inextricably interlinked.
“I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted. As a country which has suffered famine, colonisation and the violence of the Troubles, but also the importance of the long and challenging road to peace, I emphasised the unique insight which Irish people can bring to the resolution of conflict.
“I highlighted to President Trump the strong commitment which the Irish people have to international relations, to the importance of the United Nations, including the pride which Irish people feel in Ireland’s contribution to UN Peacekeeping since 1958, and to the obligations contained within Article 29 of our Constitution towards the peaceful resolution of international disputes.
“I assured President Trump that the Irish people would strongly support all those who have the strength to build a shared peace in all those parts of the world currently suffering from such horrific war and violence.”
During their discussions around the north, President Connolly noted the contribution made by the United States to the peace process, including through the International Fund for Ireland.
To mark the courtesy call, President Connolly gifted President Trump a St Brigid’s Cross, a copy of the book ‘Navigatio Sancti Brendani – The Voyage of St Brendan’, and the collected poems of Michael Longley, including his sonnet ‘Ceasefire’.

sources.news_title: Trump comment breaks precedent on Irish unification during his visit
Trump might avoid a global backlash —because no one cares what he says
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has once again stumbled "with stamping feet" into statements that hit a raw nerve internationally, but according to a new breakdown from The i Paper, he might avoid causing an incident this time around, largely because no one cares what he has to say anymore.
Trump has been visiting Ireland this weekend to attend a golf tournament and briefly meet with the country's leader, Taoiseach Micheál Martin. While the visit has seemingly been crafted to avoid diplomatic headaches, the president nonetheless managed to play with fire when he made comments expressing support for the unification of Ireland with Northern Ireland, the region on the same island controlled by the United Kingdom.
"I’d love to see it unified,” Trump said. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually... yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?"
Writing for The i Paper on Saturday, reporter and columnist James Ball said that "To call the issue a sensitive one is a dramatic understatement."
"People have fought and died for both sides of this cause for more than a century," Ball explained. "The current relatively peaceful status quo was achieved through the Northern Irish peace process, which involved painstaking, grinding diplomacy over a period of years – with significant US involvement."
Ball further argued that Trump's comments "in normal circumstances, dramatically upend the status quo." He also noted that the supporters of the current status quo have "spoken most favorably of Trump," believing him more likely than former President Joe Biden to support their cause.
Typically, such statements from a U.S. president would not be made "without significant diplomatic work alongside it," but that, Ball added, is yet another norm Trump has shattered in his second term.
"At this stage, everyone knows that isn’t how Donald Trump’s administration operates in its second term," Ball wrote. "Instead, the 80-year-old President just tends to say whatever pops into his head at any given moment, and whatever seems like a good idea at the time. If someone puts it to him in different terms later, he might say something else entirely."
Despite the potential concerns, however, Ball argued that Trump's Ireland comments are unlikely to kick up an international incident in the same way that his Greenland remarks did, as his conduct in office has severely degraded the import of his words and the weight of his office.
"Trump is so volatile that his words no longer carry the weight that they once did, and certainly not the weight that his office implies," Ball argued. "Even a few short years ago, everything he said was international news, because it could be assumed that everything he said mattered. Now, we almost always have to wait a few days to see whether Trump really means it or not."
He concluded: "Whatever Trump’s intent, any hopes for a relatively quiet weekend are surely over. Trump has made headline news on an issue that is life and death, especially for the people living in Northern Ireland. The mess he left behind will be for others to clean up, though. Trump himself has golf to watch, after all."

Trump in Dublin says he'd love to see Ireland unified
Trump's call for united Ireland draws swift rejection from pro-British unionists
President Trump Backs A United Ireland, Says It Is ‘Going To Happen Eventually’ – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Isaac
sources.text:
President Trump walked straight into one of Europe’s oldest political fault lines Saturday and said what generations of American presidents have carefully avoided saying.
During a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, President Trump said he would “love” to see the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland reunified.
Then he went further. He predicted it would happen eventually, suggested it might as well happen now and pointed to Martin as the man who could help get it moving.
The full exchange captured President Trump at his most unscripted:
BREAKING: Donald Trump has said he would 'love' to see a unified Ireland during a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin.
Replying to a reporter, the US president said 'it's going to happen eventually' adding 'the UK will have something to say about it'. pic.twitter.com/hJ2ZjdIhB5
— Sky News (@SkyNews) September 12, 2026
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at Farmleigh House.
He said he has friends on both sides of the border and called a united Ireland a potential “great feather in everybody’s cap.” Martin stood beside him as Trump added, “You’ve got the right man here to get it moving.”
Trump acknowledged that the United Kingdom would have a major say in any change, but he did not retreat from his view.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said. “How can it be bad?”
The Associated Press reports that Trump’s remarks broke sharply with the caution normally shown by American presidents on Irish reunification. Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom, while the Republic of Ireland is an independent country.
The constitutional question fueled the Troubles, three decades of violence that left roughly 3,600 people dead before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement brought most of the bloodshed to an end.
That peace agreement did not permanently settle Northern Ireland’s status. It provides a lawful path to a vote on reunification if it appears likely that a majority would support joining the Republic of Ireland.
The British government controls when such a border poll is called, which has kept the question politically explosive even as demographics and public attitudes have shifted.
What are your thoughts?
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said this week that he was not aware of majority support for another referendum and that there would not be one unless that changed. Trump effectively challenged that cautious timetable by declaring the eventual outcome inevitable and suggesting there was no reason to wait.
The president’s words carried extra weight because he delivered them beside Ireland’s head of government, on Irish soil, during a visit already drawing enormous attention. He also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, addressed American and Irish business leaders and traveled to Doonbeg for the Irish Open at his family’s golf resort.
The visit included plenty of warmth as well. One clip from Dublin showed President Trump praising the Irish people and leaning into the deep bond between Ireland and the United States:
Just Trump being a legend, speaking in Dublin today about Irish people ☘️🇮🇪😂🫱🏻🫲🏼🇺🇸
Follow us and share pic.twitter.com/O9f9gZKgTF
— TheLiberal.ie (@TheLiberal_ie) September 12, 2026
The reaction was immediate, including from one of Trump’s most prominent political allies in Britain.
Nigel Farage rejected the president’s position outright. Farage said Northern Ireland remains a proud part of the United Kingdom and argued that its people want neither a referendum nor unification:
Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom.
The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification.
I disagree with President Trump.
— Nigel Farage (@Nigel_Farage) September 12, 2026
Farage’s response shows how unusual this moment really was. Trump went beyond warm words about Irish-American friendship.
He took a clear position on a question that divides nationalists and unionists, Dublin and London, and even parts of the political right.
Whether a united Ireland comes soon, decades from now or never at all will ultimately be decided by the people who live there under the terms of the peace agreement.
But President Trump has now put the question back in the international spotlight, and he did it in a way no carefully scripted diplomat ever would.

sources.news_title: President Trump Backs A United Ireland, Says It Is ‘Going To Happen Eventually’
sources.text:
President Trump walked straight into one of Europe’s oldest political fault lines Saturday and said what generations of American presidents have carefully avoided saying.
During a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, President Trump said he would “love” to see the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland reunified.
Then he went further. He predicted it would happen eventually, suggested it might as well happen now and pointed to Martin as the man who could help get it moving.
The full exchange captured President Trump at his most unscripted:
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at Farmleigh House.
He said he has friends on both sides of the border and called a united Ireland a potential “great feather in everybody’s cap.” Martin stood beside him as Trump added, “You’ve got the right man here to get it moving.”
Trump acknowledged that the United Kingdom would have a major say in any change, but he did not retreat from his view.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said. “How can it be bad?”
The Associated Press reports that Trump’s remarks broke sharply with the caution normally shown by American presidents on Irish reunification. Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom, while the Republic of Ireland is an independent country.
The constitutional question fueled the Troubles, three decades of violence that left roughly 3,600 people dead before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement brought most of the bloodshed to an end.
That peace agreement did not permanently settle Northern Ireland’s status. It provides a lawful path to a vote on reunification if it appears likely that a majority would support joining the Republic of Ireland.
The British government controls when such a border poll is called, which has kept the question politically explosive even as demographics and public attitudes have shifted.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said this week that he was not aware of majority support for another referendum and that there would not be one unless that changed. Trump effectively challenged that cautious timetable by declaring the eventual outcome inevitable and suggesting there was no reason to wait.
The president’s words carried extra weight because he delivered them beside Ireland’s head of government, on Irish soil, during a visit already drawing enormous attention. He also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, addressed American and Irish business leaders and traveled to Doonbeg for the Irish Open at his family’s golf resort.
The visit included plenty of warmth as well. One clip from Dublin showed President Trump praising the Irish people and leaning into the deep bond between Ireland and the United States:
Just Trump being a legend, speaking in Dublin today about Irish people ☘️🇮🇪😂🫱🏻🫲🏼🇺🇸
Follow us and share pic.twitter.com/O9f9gZKgTF
The reaction was immediate, including from one of Trump’s most prominent political allies in Britain.
Nigel Farage rejected the president’s position outright. Farage said Northern Ireland remains a proud part of the United Kingdom and argued that its people want neither a referendum nor unification:
Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom. 
The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification. 
I disagree with President Trump.
Farage’s response shows how unusual this moment really was. Trump went beyond warm words about Irish-American friendship.
He took a clear position on a question that divides nationalists and unionists, Dublin and London, and even parts of the political right.
Whether a united Ireland comes soon, decades from now or never at all will ultimately be decided by the people who live there under the terms of the peace agreement.
But President Trump has now put the question back in the international spotlight, and he did it in a way no carefully scripted diplomat ever would.

sources.news_title: ‘Not as orange as he looks’: NI parties weigh Donald Trump’s united Ireland comments
sources.text:
It was, as one senior SDLP figure put it, “quite a moment, to have the American president saying that.”
The “that” in question was Donald Trump’s endorsement of Irish unity, delivered when answering questions from the media after his arrival in Ireland on Saturday.
“I’d love to see it unified”, Trump said; it would be “a fantastic thing ... a great thing” and even “a very cool thing.”
At the SDLP conference, taking place in a south Belfast hotel as Trump was speaking in Dublin, they were already talking unity.
READ MORE
The “direction of travel” towards constitutional change was “clear”, the SDLP leader Claire Hanna told the party faithful in her speech. Addressing the recent assertion by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, that a Border poll was “off the table”, Hanna responded: “A new Ireland isn’t just on the table, it’s on the move.”
Then the US president weighed in. “Donald Trump, in the last hour, has announced that he is in favour of united Ireland,” she said. “Turns out he’s not as orange as he looks,” she added, in an allusion to the Orange Order.
Her audience laughed. “I’m not sure if anybody’s checked on the DUP,” she continued. “I suspect they’re burning those Trump flags as we speak.”
But, she said, Trump’s comments underlined “as clearly as anything that change is happening, whether some parties here want to acknowledge it or not”.
On Saturday, those unionist parties disagreed, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) all issuing swift statements essentially telling Trump to keep out of it.
“Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington,” was how the DUP leader Gavin Robinson put it.
UUP deputy leader Robbie Butler took a swipe at “those now cheering” Trump, accusing them of “cherry picking.
“One sentence about a united Ireland and he is apparently a statesman of rare vision,” he said.
The former SDLP leader Colum Eastwood, a long-standing critic of the US president, had his own tongue-in-cheek response, posting a video of Trump’s comments on social media with the caption: “Always liked him.”
“I think it’s a sign of the times,” Eastwood told The Irish Times. “We had the former British prime minister Gordon Brown last week saying he thinks a united Ireland will happen, now we have the current president of America saying he thinks a united Ireland will happen.
“I think there is a recognition around the world that, after Brexit, the direction of travel was clear, that we’re heading towards Irish unity.
“That doesn’t mean that those of us that want to see it don’t have to work very hard to make sure it happens.
“Whatever about all the conversation and the distraction about criteria and dates, there is going to be a Border poll, we are going to win it, and Ireland’s going to be united ... so it’s good to see that the American president, even though I don’t agree with him very much, understands that reality.”
As Hanna said in a statement later on Saturday, “when even Donald Trump has clocked that Irish unity is no longer some distant or theoretical prospect, it tells you something about just how far this conversation has shifted”.
Or, as she put it in her speech earlier, it was “becoming clearer by the day that the future of this island is changing” and “more and more people are talking about our constitutional future.
“Don’t just take it from me,” she said. “Take it from the leader of the free world.”

sources.news_title: Trump says a united Ireland would be ‘fantastic’ during golf trip
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would “love” to see the United Kingdom’s Northern Ireland reunify with the Republic of Ireland, arguing that such a move would be “a fantastic thing” and would eventually happen.
Trump made the comments during a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin in Dublin, where the president was visiting ahead of the Irish Open at his golf resort.

“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump said. “It’s going to happen eventually.”
Trump acknowledged that the U.K. would have a say in the matter but said he believed Irish reunification “would be a great thing.”
“Now the U.K. would have something to say about it, obviously, but I think it would be a great thing,” Trump said. “I mean, how can it be bad?”
Trump was asked about the issue again later and reiterated his support, describing reunification as “a very cool thing.”
Trump also suggested that Martin was the “right man” to help advance the cause of Irish reunification.
The remarks drew a quick pushback from British and Northern Irish unionists.
Kemi Badenoch, leader of Britain’s opposition Conservative Party, accused Trump of “shooting from the hip as usual,” adding that his comments about the future of democratic countries were “deeply unhelpful” and created “unnecessary tension.”
Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson rejected Trump’s comments, saying Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people.
“Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington,” Robinson said. He added that Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom because of the “settled democratic will of its people.”
Sinn Fein leader Mary Lou McDonald, meanwhile, welcomed Trump’s remarks and said the Irish government should begin preparing for reunification.
“Our national journey is now reunification, which is organised, planned and a peaceful transition,” McDonald said.
Trump’s comments come as the British government has recently faced questions over its position on a referendum on Irish reunification.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in August that a referendum on a united Ireland was “off the table” during his first official visit to Northern Ireland. He later clarified his position in Parliament, saying he would “stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100%.”

The 1998 Good Friday Agreement ended decades of violence known as the Troubles and established a legal framework for determining Northern Ireland’s future. Under the agreement, the British government is required to hold a referendum on Irish reunification if the Northern Ireland secretary determines that a majority of voters would likely support it.
Trump also praised the U.S.-Ireland relationship during his meeting with Martin, saying the two countries have “a big relationship” and that the relationship “has never been as good as it is right now.”

sources.news_title: Trump's united Ireland remarks draw sharp response from British unionists
sources.text:
Trump's united Ireland remarks draw sharp response from British unionists
- By Reuters -
- Sep 12, 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he would “love” to see British-run Northern Ireland unify with Ireland, remarks made during a visit to Dublin that drew a sharp response from pro-British unionists in Northern Ireland.
Trump’s comments come weeks after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was “off the table”, a position Downing Street on Saturday said remained unchanged.
“Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters sitting next to Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin after the pair met in Dublin. “It’s going to happen eventually … I think it would be a fantastic thing.”
“Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing,” he added.
COMMENTS BREAK WITH NEUTRAL STANCE OF PREVIOUS PRESIDENTS
Trump later said that there “was no good answer” to the question on Irish unity but repeated that he thought it would be “a very cool thing”.
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, a referendum can be held only at the discretion of the British government. The accord ended three decades of violence between Irish nationalists seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the UK.
While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain’s departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.
The leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, Northern Ireland’s largest party advocating continued union with Britain, rejected Trump’s prediction, saying unification with Ireland would lead to “the destruction of our country.”
“Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington,” Gavin Robinson, who has publicly supported Trump in the past, wrote on X.
In Belfast, supporters of Irish unity gave a guarded response.
“I think it’s just headline grabbing … I don’t think he gives a toss whether there is a United Ireland or not,” said Eamon Hanna, a supporter of the nationalist SDLP party, which has been a strong critic of Trump’s policies.
Previous U.S. presidents, including those with strong Irish heritage like Joe Biden, have been careful to remain neutral on Irish unification. The U.S. government played a key role in brokering the 1998 peace deal.
‘YOU FLEECED US’
Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who had joined a protest against his 2019 visit to Ireland, before she was elected to the mostly ceremonial role last year.
Connolly, formerly a long-time left-wing lawmaker, said in a statement that she conveyed to Trump “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted.”
Her statement did not reference any conflict, but she has been previously critical of the U.S. war with Iran and Israel’s assault on Gaza, which Ireland, in common with a U.N. inquiry and several human rights groups, has described as a genocide.
Israel rejects that characterisation, saying that it is fighting the militants who attacked it from the Palestinian enclave in 2023.
Thousands of protesters, some holding posters calling Trump a warmonger and chanting “Free free Palestine”, marched through central Dublin shortly after Trump left to watch a golf tournament at one of his resorts in the west of Ireland.
It was one of the country’s largest anti-war protests in recent years.
The centrist premier Martin had earlier focused his remarks on the countries’ close economic ties. U.S.-owned companies, mainly in the technology and pharmaceutical sectors, employ about 10% of workers in Ireland after successive governments prioritized the companies’ jobs and tax revenues over decades.
“You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back,” Trump said.
“You fleeced us but that’s okay … There’s a lot of room to go around and our relationship with you is fantastic.”

sources.news_title: President Donald Trump touches a nerve while in Ireland by saying reunification would be ‘fantastic’
sources.text:
DUBLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” as he waded into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a major tournament at his Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the United Kingdom’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told a reporter who sought his opinion on the issue. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” the Republican president said, adding that “the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”
At his next stop, Trump acknowledged there is “no good answer” to the reunification question as he addressed business leaders from both countries gathered at the U.S. ambassador’s residence.
The Irish unity debate is heated
Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether Irish or British — drove decades of violence in the six-county region that has a Protestant majority and has remained part of the U.K.
Previous American presidents, including Democrat Joe Biden, who has strong emotional ties to Ireland, have avoided commenting directly on the subject.
Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbor Britain, became a self-governing Catholic-majority country a century ago. Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists, most of them Catholic, who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.
A 1998 peace accord that the United States was instrumental in negotiating largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved. That agreement allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the U.K. would only consider allowing a referendum “when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered.” Burnham’s office referred back to that comment when asked about Trump’s statement.
Trump’s comments Saturday, along with recent statements about the Falkland Islands, a small British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean that Argentina calls Las Malvinas, could also be viewed as a dig at Britain, given his anger over London’s refusal to be drawn into the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Trump also talked about the Falkland Islands
Trump once more raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falklands. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has recently restated his country’s claim to the territory of about 3,500 people, which is about 300 miles (480 kilometers) east of the southeast coast of Argentina.
Trump has previously said Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. On Saturday, he expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the Falklands as it did after Argentina invaded in 1982.
“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out,” he said.
A meeting with the Irish president who criticized Trump
Trump also held talks in Dublin with Irish President Catherine Connolly, a left-wing politician who joined protesters when Trump visited Ireland in 2019 during his first term in office. She is now Ireland’s elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, Connolly has in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a “bully.”
Connolly said in a statement after the meeting that she conveyed to Trump “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalization of war and genocide can never be accepted.” She gave Trump several gifts, among them a collection by the late Irish poet Michael Longley that includes the sonnet “Ceasefire.”
Asked about the meeting, Trump first had his protocol chief, Monica Crowley, answer before he was pressed and said it was “very nice.” “We discussed a lot of things, quickly,” Trump said.

Trump also raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falkland Islands.
DUBLIN (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a major tournament at his Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the U.K.’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump offered when asked for his opinion on the issue by a reporter. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said, adding that “the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”
The Irish unity debate is heated
Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether it’s Irish or British — drove decades of violence in Northern Ireland that left some 3,600 people dead. Previous American presidents have avoided commenting directly on the subject, even those, like Joe Biden, with strong emotional ties to Ireland.
When Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbor Britain, became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country a century ago, a six-county region in the north with a Protestant majority remained part of the United Kingdom.
Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles: three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.
A 1998 peace accord that the U.S. was instrumental in striking largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved.
The peace accord allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that “I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one.”
Trump also talked about the Falkland Islands issue
Trump again raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falkland Islands. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has recently restated Argentina’s claim to the islands, a British overseas territory that Argentina calls Las Malvinas.
Trump has previously said Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. On Saturday he expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the South Atlantic islands as they did after Argentina invaded in 1982.
“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out,” he said.
A meeting with the Irish president who criticized Trump
Trump also held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart Catherine Connolly and will address U.S. and Irish business leaders at the U.S. ambassador’s official residence in Dublin, before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open.
Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019, during his first term in office. She is now Ireland’s elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a “bully.”
The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the U.S. national anthem and inspected an Irish Army honor guard.
Trump visit irks some Dubliners
Police put up a cordon around Dublin’s 1,750-acre (700-hectare) Phoenix Park, where he met Connolly at her residence, Áras an Uachtaráin. He met Martin, the taoiseach, at the government’s Farmleigh state guesthouse and stopped by Deerfield, the U.S. ambassador’s residence.
Some residents expressed annoyance over the disruption.
“He’s causing mayhem in this city because he wants to go down to Doonbeg and play golf,” said taxi driver Christopher Fox, emphatically not a fan of Trump. “The world’s in turmoil and this fella’s down playing golf.”
University student Mina Petrovski said Trump’s “attitudes toward women, toward immigrants, toward minority communities in general are abhorrent.” She said it’s “shameful that the Irish government is welcoming him with open arms.”
Separately, a collection of left-leaning opposition parties, anti-military groups, pro-Palestinian organizations, environmentalists and others plan to demonstrate against Trump in Dublin on Saturday.
Eric Trump defends family’s presence in Ireland
Trump’s son, Eric, says the family is loved in Ireland, despite the protests planned over his father’s visit.
Speaking to Irish national broadcaster RTE on Friday in Doonbeg, home to the Trump International golf resort, Eric Trump said the course is the largest employer in the area.
“Go down to Morrissey’s tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family, go have them attest to what we’ve done for the country and what we’ve invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them,” he said.
Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.
Trump plays golf just about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.
The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump’s golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.
Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. During that visit, he held talks with the British prime minister and the president of the European Commission.

sources.news_title: Northern Ireland unionist leaders criticise Donald Trump after he said he would “love to see” a United Ireland
sources.text:
Donald Trump’s united Ireland comments spark unionist backlash
Unionist leaders in Northern Ireland have criticised US President Donald Trump after he said he would “love to see” a united Ireland.
Mr Trump was speaking alongside Taoiseach Micheal Martin when he was asked for his view on a united Ireland, and said it was “going to happen eventually, it may as well happen now”.
Later, speaking at the US ambassador’s residence in Ireland, Mr Trump discussed the Press Association’s question, saying: “They’re going for the kill at all times, and they ask me a question: ‘What do you think about unification of Northern Ireland and Ireland?’
“That was one of the questions. But I actually said it would be, I think, a very cool thing. To be honest with you, I think it would be cool.”
Earlier this year, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham sparked a political row on the island of Ireland when he said a unity referendum is “off the table”.
Under the terms of the 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement, the UK secretary of state can decide to hold a border poll, and it also places a duty on the office holder to call one if it appears likely a majority would vote for Irish unification.
The people of the Republic of Ireland must also vote in favour to effect constitutional change.
Republican party Sinn Fein has boycotted the annual St Patrick’s day visit to Washington for the last two years over the current administration’s stance on the Middle East.
However, Northern Ireland’s leading unionist parties, the DUP and UUP, have continued to attend and engage with Mr Trump, and the DUP Communities Minister Gordon Lyons hosted an event on Capitol Hill to mark the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
On Saturday DUP leader Gavin Robinson posted on X: “President Trump knows better than most that elections matter.
“Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.
“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people.
“I am confident NI will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic.”
TUV leader Jim Allister said Mr Trump “is not the first US president to meddle in the affairs which don’t concern him”.
He added: “Northern Ireland is not a pawn in Trump’s fall-out with the UK. Our constitutional future does not depend on him or any other foreign dignitary.”
Ulster Unionist Party Leader Jon Burrows MLA said the US president “like anyone else in the world, is entitled to express his view on the constitutional future of another country”.
“But the only people whose decision counts are the people of Northern Ireland,” he said.
“That is the principle of consent, now enshrined in law through the Belfast Agreement, negotiated and delivered by the Ulster Unionist Party.
“America has been, and remains, an important ally, from the Second World War and the global fight against terrorism to the defence of democracy around the world. Their businesses increasingly see that our workforce here is the best in the world.
“But when all is said and done, Northern Ireland’s future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland.
“I am confident that we are safer, more secure and more prosperous within the United Kingdom, and that is where we will remain.”
Former SDLP leader and MP for Foyle Colum Eastwood, an open critic of the US president, shared a clip of Mr Trump’s remarks on social media adding: “Always liked him.”
UUP MLA Robbie Butler MLA said there was a “sudden conversion” from some of Mr Trump’s opponents.
“For years we have been told this president is beyond the pale: his character, his conduct, his position on Gaza,” he said.
“Some of those now cheering him boycotted the White House over it. One sentence about a united Ireland and he is apparently a statesman of rare vision.
“It seems his judgment is sound only on the one subject where it happens to suit. The cherry picking is at least consistent.”

Trump would 'love' to see a united Ireland, he says in Dublin stop
DUBLIN – President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would "love" to see British-run Northern Ireland unify with Ireland, remarks made during a visit to Dublin that drew a sharp response from pro-British unionists in Northern Ireland.
Trump's comments come weeks after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was "off the table," a position Downing Street on Saturday said remained unchanged.
"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters sitting next to Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin after the pair met in Dublin. "It's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing."
'A very cool thing'
"Now the U.K. will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing," he added.
Trump later said that there "was no good answer" to the question on Irish unity but repeated that he thought it would be "a very cool thing."
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the U.K. can be held only at the discretion of the British government. The accord ended three decades of violence between Irish nationalists seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the U.K.
While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favor remaining in the U.K., the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain's departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.
The leader of Northern Ireland's largest unionist party, the Democratic Unionist Party, rejected Trump's prediction, saying unification would lead to "the destruction of our country."
"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," Gavin Robinson, who has publicly supported Trump in the past, wrote on X.
Previous U.S. presidents, including those with strong Irish heritage like Joe Biden, have been careful to remain neutral on Irish unification. The U.S. government played a key role in brokering the 1998 peace deal.

Trump is making the 48-hour trip as his Republican Party campaigns to retain its majorities in both chambers of Congress. He is due to attend a golf tournament at one of his resorts later Saturday.
Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who was elected head of state last year. When Trump last visited Ireland as president in 2019, Connolly, an outspoken politician with far-left foreign policy views, protested outside Shannon Airport in western Ireland.

sources.news_title: Trump wades into united Ireland controversy with stamping feet
sources.text:
Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland this weekend was supposed to be a quiet trip to watch a golf tournament.
There was no major summit, no plans for a big event and Irish politicians had made it clear their primary goal for Trump’s trip was to get through it without any major diplomatic incidents.
For the first hour or two, things seemed to be going to plan. Trump’s agreed itinerary kept him away from potential crowds of protestors, and he was given a relatively low-key greeting by the President and Taoiseach. All that remained was a short press Q&A session before Trump could go and watch his golf.
And then, Donald Trump declared his support for Irish reunification. “I’d love to see it unified,” he said. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually…yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.
“Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
To call the issue a sensitive one is a dramatic understatement: people have fought and died for both sides of this cause for more than a century. The current relatively peaceful status quo was achieved through the Northern Irish peace process, which involved painstaking, grinding diplomacy over a period of years – with significant US involvement.
There has always been more US awareness of the Northern Irish troubles than many other European conflicts: the UK is one of the USA’s closest military allies, and its closest intelligence partner across the world. But many Americans have Irish ancestry, and the two countries have long celebrated that bond.
As a result, president Clinton was deeply involved in brokering the Good Friday Agreement, carefully picking every word he said, and pushing both sides behind the scenes to make concessions, in a delicately managed process.
Donald Trump, by contrast, has waded in largely unasked with huge, stamping feet. Though the Good Friday Agreement has endured for nearly 30 years, it has been under pressure in recent years – Brexit tested its terms, and the possibility of the UK leaving key mechanisms like the European Court of Human Rights could challenge it further.
The US President seemingly declaring his strong support for one side would, in normal circumstances, dramatically upend the status quo – not least because Northern Ireland’s loyalists are the faction which has spoken most favourably of Trump, who they thought would be more on their side than Biden, a Catholic president with Irish heritage.
But generally, no normal US president would make a pronouncement like Trump’s without significant diplomatic work alongside it. His team would have laid groundwork with key officials in the UK and Irish governments. There would be a communications plan, and a rationale. Diplomats would have worked on it for weeks. It would be a statement of intent.
At this stage, everyone knows that isn’t how Donald Trump’s administration operates in its second term. Instead, the 80-year-old President just tends to say whatever pops into his head at any given moment, and whatever seems like a good idea at the time. If someone puts it to him in different terms later, he might say something else entirely.
Trump might even argue he didn’t say who Ireland should be united under. The obvious implication of his statement is an independent, unified island of Ireland. But the chaotic President might argue he meant it should all be part of the UK, since everyone’s friends now. More likely, he might suddenly decide that Ireland – like Greenland – would make a great addition to the USA, and offer it statehood.
Trump is so volatile that his words no longer carry the weight that they once did, and certainly not the weight that his office implies. Even a few short years ago, everything he said was international news, because it could be assumed that everything he said mattered. Now, we almost always have to wait a few days to see whether Trump really means it or not.
Whatever Trump’s intent, any hopes for a relatively quiet weekend are surely over. Trump has made headline news on an issue that is life and death, especially for the people living in Northern Ireland. The mess he left behind will be for others to clean up, though. Trump himself has golf to watch, after all.

sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” as he waded into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a major tournament at his Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the United Kingdom’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told a reporter who sought his opinion on the issue. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” the Republican president said, adding that “the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”
At his next stop, Trump acknowledged there is “no good answer” to the reunification question as he addressed business leaders from both countries gathered at the U.S. ambassador’s residence.
Competing visions of Northern Ireland – whether Irish or British – drove decades of violence in the six-county region that has a Protestant majority and has remained part of the U.K.
Previous American presidents, including Democrat Joe Biden, who has strong emotional ties to Ireland, have avoided commenting directly on the subject.
Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbour Britain, became a self-governing Catholic-majority country a century ago. Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists, most of them Catholic, who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.
Hardball stance with Trump sets Canada apart from all the trading partners that acquiesced
A 1998 peace accord that the United States was instrumental in negotiating largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved. That agreement allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the U.K. would only consider allowing a referendum “when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered.” Burnham’s office referred back to that comment when asked about Trump’s statement.
During the same visit, Trump told reporters that Canada was keen to reach a trade deal with the United States and that an agreement could come “fairly soon,” while repeating complaints that Canada had treated U.S. farmers unfairly and should remove tariffs.
“Canada wants to make a deal very badly,” he said.
“Canada has to treat our farmers better. They can’t charge our farmers tariffs,” Trump said, adding: “You’ll probably see a deal with Canada fairly soon.”
Trump’s comments Saturday, along with recent statements about the Falkland Islands, a small British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean that Argentina calls Las Malvinas, could also be viewed as a dig at Britain, given his anger over London’s refusal to be drawn into the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Trump also talked about the Falkland Islands
Trump once more raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falklands. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has recently restated his country’s claim to the territory of about 3,500 people, which is about 480 kilometres east of the southeast coast of Argentina.
Trump has previously said Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. On Saturday, he expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the Falklands as it did after Argentina invaded in 1982.
“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out,” he said.
A meeting with the Irish president who criticized Trump
Trump also held talks in Dublin with Irish President Catherine Connolly, a left-wing politician who joined protesters when Trump visited Ireland in 2019 during his first term in office. She is now Ireland’s elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, Connolly has in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a “bully.”
Connolly said in a statement after the meeting that she conveyed to Trump “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalization of war and genocide can never be accepted.” She gave Trump several gifts, among them a collection by the late Irish poet Michael Longley that includes the sonnet “Ceasefire.”
Asked about the meeting, Trump first had his protocol chief, Monica Crowley, answer before he was pressed and said it was “very nice.” “We discussed a lot of things, quickly,” Trump said.

Police put up a cordon around Dublin’s 1,750-acre Phoenix Park, where Connolly, Martin and U.S. Ambassador Edward Walsh have residences and welcomed Trump.
A protest march drew thousands to central Dublin. He had left the city and was on the way to his Doonbeg golf course on the country’s Atlantic coast by the time the demonstration began.
Many in the crowd waved Irish or Palestinian flags and chanted “Donald Trump not welcome here” and “Irish government, shame on you!”
Paula Butler said she came with a contingent from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre to oppose the American president’s “attitude to women, to refugees, to migrants.”
She was unimpressed by Trump’s support for Irish unity, a popular cause in Ireland.
“What he knows about Irish unity, I’d say I know more on my little finger,” Butler said.
Kim Mathis, who moved from Florida to Dublin last year with her partner, said “part of the reason we moved to Ireland was to get away from Trump and all of his horrific policies.”
She said dealing with Trump is “a global conundrum” for governments. “It would be really nice if politicians would just say, ‘Stay home.’”

Speaking to Irish national broadcaster RTE on Friday in Doonbeg, Trump’s son Eric said the course is the largest employer in the area.
“Go down to Morrissey’s tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family, go have them attest to what we’ve done for the country and what we’ve invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them,” he said.

He spends most weekends playing golf at his clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have hosted professional golf tournaments this year.
Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. During that visit, he held talks with the British prime minister and the president of the European Commission.

US President Donald Trump has said he would "love" to see the Republic of Ireland, an EU member, unite with British-run Northern Ireland as he faced reporters' questions on a range of issues on Saturday.
Trump is taking the weekend trip largely to watch the Irish Open golf tournament held on a course he owns on the country’s Atlantic coast, but he met as well with the Irish president and prime minister, or taoiseach.
The US leader also spoke optimistically about his country's war with Iran and its trade conflict with Canada, among several other topics.
What did Trump say about Ireland?
After a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in the capital, Dublin, Trump said he very much supported what he said would be the eventual unification of the two parts of the island of Ireland.
"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters.
"The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing," he added.
"Now the UK will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing."
The British government responded swiftly to the remarks, with Prime Minister Andy Burham's office saying that in his view, there was no majority public support for a referendum on the issue and that there would not be another one until that changed.
Previous US presidents have avoided touching on the subject in view of the delicate nature of the issue, with Northern Ireland seeing decades of of deadly sectarian violence in the 20th century over the question of whom it should belong to.
What did Trump say about the Iran war?
Trump also said that the US war with Iran, which began on February 28, would "end very soon" — a view he has frequently expressed in the past, but which has not yet materialized.
He also said that the end of the conflict would mean that the price of oil, which has soared as a result of the war, would "come tumbling down."
However, he vehemently defended his decision to mount the military operation against Iran.
He said that the US attacked because "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon", adding: "They were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."
"If they had it, they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East, and they would have hit some [...] in my opinion, [of] Europe's cities and beyond cities, and they would probably hit us soon before we put out the fire. But they cannot have a nuclear weapon."
The war with Iran is not supported by a majority of the US population, particularly in view of promises made by Trump on the campaign trail to keep his country out of foreign "forever" conflicts.
What did Trump say about Canada?
The president sounded a similarly optimistic note regarding the US trade war with Canada.
He said Canada was keen to make a deal and that one could be struck "fairly soon," while reiterating his claims that Canada had treated US farmers unfairly with its tariffs.
"Canada wants to make a deal very badly," he said.
"Canada has to treat our farmers better. They can't charge our farmers tariffs," he said, adding: "You'll probably see a deal with Canada fairly soon."

The Republic of Ireland gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, while Northern Ireland, established in 1921, has remained part of the U.K.
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified. I have friends on both sides, great people. They’re Irish people. He added that the U.K. “will have something to say about it obviously,” but reiterated that unification would be a “great thing.”

In response to Trump’s comments, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement that the U.K. government’s stance on reunification remains unchanged.

The debate over whether Ireland should be one country has been one of the island’s most divisive political issues for decades.
At times, it was far more than a war of words. From the late 1960s through the late 1990s, Northern Ireland was gripped by decades of sectarian violence known as “the Troubles.”
Irish nationalists and republicans — drawn largely from Northern Ireland’s Catholic minority — sought to reunite the island under a single Irish state.
Unionists and loyalists, who mostly belonged to the Protestant majority, wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the U.K.
Throughout the conflict, more than 3,500 people were killed in violence involving Irish republican and loyalist paramilitary groups, as well as British security forces.

A 2024 U.K. Parliament report found that 90% of students in Northern Ireland attend schools that “are effectively segregated along religious lines.”
The peace deal signed in 1998 — known as the Good Friday Agreement or the Belfast Agreement — set up a new government that had representation for both nationalists and unionists.
It also established that Northern Ireland will remain part of the U.K. unless a majority of citizens vote to leave through a referendum.
Brexit reignited debate over Ireland’s future, with Northern Ireland voting to remain in the European Union even as the U.K. as a whole voted to leave. Still, no referendum has been proposed or scheduled on whether Northern Ireland should leave the United Kingdom.
